notes.title: Start here: HyperNova, a site that is also a teaching repo
notes.body:
HyperNova is a Next.js marketing site with an AI project estimator: a visitor answers some questions, the site shows a quick local estimate, then an AWS (Amplify / AppSync) backend fills in an AI analysis later. The repo is also written to be read: its commits, PRs and guides teach team habits.

Suggested reading order:

1. `CONTRIBUTING.md` from top to bottom. It is short and most quizzes in this pack come from it: the branch-to-merge loop, commit messages, pull requests, review labels, the definition of done, and repo-specific rules.
2. `SECURITY.md`: where secrets live, why some environment variables are public, and what to do if a secret is committed.
3. `fabledocs/01-app-architecture-guide.md`. Read the status note at the top first: the guide describes the code *as inherited*, and many issues it lists were fixed later. Then read the estimator sections (§6) and the data model and security sections.

For the estimator questions, keep `lib/estimatorMath.ts`, `components/ProjectEstimator.tsx` and the GraphQL schema open; they carry long comments explaining each fix.

**Read `fabledocs/01-app-architecture-guide.md` before your first change.**

notes.title: Commits, pull requests and reviews in this repo
notes.body:
`CONTRIBUTING.md` treats history as something people read later. A few habits carry most of the weight:

- **Conventional Commits.** Every subject looks like `type(scope): summary`, for example `fix(api): ...`. The type says what kind of change it is (feat, fix, refactor, chore, docs, test, perf).
- **Subject vs body.** The subject is short and imperative ("stop polling...", not "stopped polling"). The body is for the reasoning the diff cannot show. Read the example body for `applyProjectToState` and notice what each paragraph is for.
- **Small PRs.** One PR per story; past about 400 lines, ask what could ship separately.
- **Review labels.** Reviewers prefix comments so the author knows what holds up the merge and what is only advice. Learn the four labels and what each covers.
- **Definition of done.** A checklist, not "it runs on my machine". The last item is about honesty with scope.

When you read the merge section, ask what someone reading `git log` a year later would see.

excerpts.quote: We use [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/): `type(scope): summary`.
**Keep them small.** A 200-line PR gets a real review; a 2,000-line PR gets "LGTM".
A story is done when *all* of these are true — not when the code runs on your machine:

readMore.why: The commit section with good and bad subject examples.

notes.title: Security model: a backend reached with anonymous credentials
notes.body:
The estimator talks to an AWS AppSync GraphQL API using **anonymous guest credentials** from a Cognito identity pool. Those credentials are inside the JavaScript sent to every browser, so anyone who opens devtools has them. That means the API's authorization rules are the only thing protecting the data.

Three ideas to carry into the quizzes:

- **Generated operations.** In Amplify, `@model` on a type generates a table plus all the standard operations for it. An `@auth` rule decides which of them guests may call. Read the schema's top comment for what the old rule granted.
- **Least privilege.** The fixed schema starts from nothing and grants only the operations the app really uses, with a comment explaining each one granted and each one withheld.
- **Public build variables.** In Next.js, variables starting with `NEXT_PUBLIC_` end up in the browser too. `SECURITY.md` explains what that means for credentials.

The architecture guide's issue table (§12) lists what was wrong as inherited; the code comments explain each fix.

excerpts.quote: Those # credentials ship inside the JavaScript bundle: every visitor has them, and so # does anyone who opens devtools.
The principle # is least privilege: start from nothing and add the specific operations the # product needs

readMore.why: The commented authorization rules for each model.
The table of issues found in the inherited code.

notes.title: Where the story id goes
notes.body:
The key is right: the story id goes in the **branch name** and the **commit body**, not the subject. Branch names follow the pattern type, then story id, then a short slug, such as `feat/HN-01-resume-estimate-link`; the guide says the id makes branch, commits and PR searchable together. For commits it says plainly: reference the story in the body (`Implements HN-01.`), not the subject. The subject stays a clean Conventional Commit summary.

Why the others are wrong:
- "In the PR title only, branches generic": branch names are required to carry the id.
- "Nowhere; the template links it": the branch format itself contains the id, and the guide asks for it in the body.
- "As a prefix in the subject": that is exactly what "not the subject" rules out, and it would break the `type(scope): summary` format.

excerpts.quote: the story id makes the branch, commits and PR searchable together.
**Reference the story** in the body (`Implements HN-01.`, `Part of HN-06.`), not the subject.

notes.title: The first move after a secret is pushed
notes.body:
The key is right: rotate the credential first, then untrack and ignore the file. Once a secret is pushed, deleting the file later does not remove it: it is still in the history, in every clone and in any fork. **Rotating** means revoking the old value and issuing a new one, so the leaked copy stops working. `SECURITY.md` says that until the old value is revoked, nothing else you do matters.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Nothing more; the delete removed it": the old commit still contains the file.
- "Rewrite history and force-push": that is step 3, optional, and it cannot reach copies already cloned or forked; the token stays valid until rotated.
- "Add it to .gitignore": ignoring only affects future commits; the leaked value is still live.

excerpts.quote: Deleting the file in a later commit **does not** remove the secret — it is still in the history, in every clone, and in any fork.
1. **Rotate the credential first.** Until the old value is revoked, nothing else you do matters. 2. Remove the file from tracking (`git rm --cached`) and add it to `.gitignore`.

notes.title: Why NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables cannot hold secrets
notes.body:
The key is right: they are inlined into the bundle at build time and readable in devtools. "Inlined" means the build replaces each use of the variable with its actual value inside the JavaScript file sent to browsers. Anyone can open devtools and read it. `CONTRIBUTING.md` puts it bluntly: treat them as if printed on the homepage.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Printed in the Amplify build console": the documented risk is the bundle every visitor downloads, not a build log.
- "The Amplify CLI commits them": nothing in the docs says so; secrets are set in the Amplify console, not committed.
- "They exist only on the server": the opposite; the prefix is what makes a variable reach the browser. Server-only secrets go through `lib/serverEnv.ts`.

excerpts.quote: Variables prefixed `NEXT_PUBLIC_` are inlined into the JavaScript bundle at build time and are readable by anyone with devtools. They are configuration, not secrets.
treat them as if printed on the homepage, because they are.
Server-side secrets are read through `lib/serverEnv.ts`

notes.title: Why a commit message with "and" should be split
notes.body:
The key is right: split it into two commits. The guide's rule is **one commit = one idea**: if you cannot describe a commit in one sentence without "and", split it. "Stop polling after the subscription delivers" is a behaviour fix; "rename the GanttChart props" is an unrelated rename. A reviewer going commit by commit should never hold two unrelated changes at once. Notice that the guide's own good-subject example is just the first half.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Keep one commit; same scope": sharing a scope does not make them one idea.
- "Move the rename into the body": the body explains *why*; it does not hide a second change.
- "Squash into the next commit": that mixes even more changes, the opposite of the rule.

excerpts.quote: **One commit = one idea.** If you can't describe it in a single sentence without "and", split it. A reviewer reading commit-by-commit should never have to hold two unrelated changes in their head.
✅ fix(estimator): stop polling after the subscription delivers

notes.title: Why an @auth rule without operations was dangerous
notes.body:
The key is right: leaving out `operations` grants guests create, read, update and delete. `@model` generates the full set of resolvers for a type: create, get and list, update, delete, plus subscriptions. The `@auth` rule `allow: public, provider: identityPool` with no `operations` list allows **all** of them to anyone holding the guest credentials, and every visitor has those. So anyone could call `listLeads` and read every submitted name and email, or call `deleteProject`.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Forced visitors to sign in": `allow: public` is the opposite; it lets anonymous guests in.
- "Reads public, writes protected": with no operations named, writes were open too; `deleteProject` is the example.
- "Blocked subscriptions": subscriptions were allowed too; that is what let a later bug leak updates.

excerpts.quote: with no `operations`, which grants all of them. @model generates create, # read (get + list), update and delete resolvers plus subscriptions, so that # rule meant any anonymous visitor could call listLeads
means **any anonymous visitor with guest credentials can call every generated operation**, including `listLeads` and `deleteProject`.

notes.title: What a commit body is for
notes.body:
The key is right: the reason for the change, why now, and the intended behaviour change. The guide's heading is "The body explains WHY, not WHAT", because the diff already shows what changed. Its example body for `applyProjectToState` names the bug the duplicated code caused, says the refactor is needed now for HN-01, and flags the one intended behaviour change so a reviewer knows it is not an accident.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Test output and lint results": the definition of done asks you to run them; the body is for reasoning, not logs.
- "Nothing; the subject is enough": the subject is a 72-character summary and cannot hold the reasoning.
- "A file-by-file list": that is the WHAT, which the diff already shows.

excerpts.quote: **The body explains WHY, not WHAT.** The diff already shows what changed.
it names the bug the duplication *caused*, explains why the refactor is happening *now*, and flags the one intentional behaviour change

notes.title: Labelling review comments: blocking or nit
notes.body:
The key is right: the missing test is **blocking**, the naming choice is a **nit**. The guide lists what counts as blocking: correctness, security, data loss, and missing tests for new logic. A different variable name is style and taste, which is a nit; you say `nit:` and let the author decide. The definition of done backs this up: new logic has tests.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Naming blocking, test a question": this reverses the two; you already know the test is missing, so it is not a question.
- "Both nits; tests can come later": missing tests for new logic is on the blocking list.
- "Both blocking": that would hold up the merge over taste, which the labels exist to avoid.

excerpts.quote: - **blocking:** correctness, security, data loss, missing tests for new logic. - **nit:** style and taste. Say `nit:` explicitly and let the author decide.
New logic has tests. Bug fixes have a test that fails without the fix.

notes.title: Why the estimator posts to a URL ending in a slash
notes.body:
The key is right: without the slash, the request is redirected and the POST body is lost. `next.config.mjs` sets `trailingSlash: true`, so Next.js redirects `/api/create-hubspot-lead` to `/api/create-hubspot-lead/`. A browser following that kind of redirect does not resend the form data, so the API would get an empty request. The fetch call in `ProjectEstimator.tsx` has a comment saying exactly this.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Bypasses the rate limiter": nothing about the slash touches rate limiting.
- "Pages Router returns 404 without the slash": the problem is a redirect, not a 404.
- "HubSpot rejects URLs without a slash": this URL is the site's own API route, not HubSpot's; HubSpot is called later from the server.

excerpts.quote: trailingSlash: true,
// Note: next.config.mjs sets `trailingSlash: true`, so use a trailing slash to avoid a redirect. const hubspotResponse = await fetch('/api/create-hubspot-lead/', {
Internal `fetch` calls to API routes must include the trailing slash (`/api/create-hubspot-lead/`) or the POST body is lost to a redirect.

notes.title: Why PRs are merged with merge commits
notes.body:
The key is right: so `git log --first-parent` reads as a list of shipped stories. A merge commit (`--no-ff`) keeps each story's commits together under one "Merge PR #n" commit. `--first-parent` follows only those merge commits on `main`, giving one line per story. The architecture guide confirms the result: the merge history, `Merge PR #1` through `Merge PR #19`, names every story HN-01 to HN-20.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Keeps each commit's original author": that is not the reason the guide gives.
- "History stays strictly linear": merge commits make history *non*-linear; linear history is what rebase gives.
- "Amplify refuses rebased branches": nothing in the repo says so.

excerpts.quote: Use **merge commits** in this repo (`--no-ff`) so each story stays a legible unit in the history and `git log --first-parent` reads as a list of shipped stories.
repository's merge history (`Merge PR #1` … `Merge PR #19`, local merges —

notes.title: What parseTimelineToMonths does with a range and with ASAP
notes.body:
The key is right: 5 and 12. For "4-6 months", the regex `/\d+/g` finds two numbers, 4 and 6. With two numbers the code averages the first two: `Math.round((4 + 6) / 2)` = 5. The text contains "month", so it returns 5. For "ASAP" there are no digits at all, so `nums.length === 0` and it returns 12. The doc comment explains the 12: a deliberately cautious guess, because under-estimating a timeline under-estimates the cost.

Why the others are wrong:
- "4 and 0": the code averages a range rather than taking the first number, and there is no path that returns 0 for missing digits.
- "5 and NaN": the no-digit case is handled before any parsing, so no NaN.
- "6 and 1": it does not take the larger number, and the default is 12, not 1.

excerpts.quote: const nums = (timeline.match(/\d+/g) || []).map((n) => parseInt(n, 10)) if (nums.length === 0) return 12
const n = nums.length === 1 ? nums[0] : Math.round((nums[0] + nums[1]) / 2)
Defaults to 12 months when it cannot tell -- a deliberately conservative * guess, since under-estimating a timeline produces an under-estimated cost

notes.title: What "done" means when one criterion cannot be met
notes.body:
The key is right: record the unfinished criterion in the PR or a follow-up issue. The definition of done lists "every acceptance criterion is demonstrably met", and its last item covers the case where you cannot: anything you could not finish is written down, in the PR or as a follow-up issue. The guide calls silent scope reduction the most expensive habit on the list.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Hold the PR open until the property exists": the guide does not ask you to block finished work on an outside dependency; it asks you to write the gap down.
- "Drop the criterion from the story": that is silent scope reduction, exactly the habit named as most expensive.
- "Mark it done anyway": the criterion is not met and nothing records it, so the story fails the checklist.

excerpts.quote: Anything you *couldn't* finish is written down — in the PR, or as a follow-up issue. Silent scope reduction is the most expensive habit on this list.
Every acceptance criterion in the story is demonstrably met.

notes.title: Why granting get but not list protects estimates
notes.body:
The key is right: the project id acts as a capability token. With `get` allowed, anyone who knows an id can read that one estimate; that is needed for polling and for shareable links. Without `list`, nobody can ask for *all* projects. So knowing the id is what grants access, like a key. The schema comment says exactly this, and warns never to build a UI that enumerates ids.

Why the others are wrong:
- "A public identifier safe to list, share and cache": list is withheld precisely because ids must not be enumerated.
- "AppSync encrypts it": nothing in the schema or guide describes encrypting ids.
- "None; get and list are equivalent": they are not. `list` returns every visitor's scope and budget without knowing any id; `get` needs the id first.

excerpts.quote: That id is the only thing # protecting a given estimate, so treat it as a capability token and # never build a UI that enumerates ids.
nothing in the product lists projects, and it would expose every # visitor's scope description and budget to anyone who asked.
operations: [create, get, listen]

notes.title: What was wrong with the unfiltered subscription
notes.body:
The key is right: each visitor's browser received other visitors' project updates. Subscribing to `onUpdateProject` with no `variables` asks AppSync for **every** project update. The browser then dropped the ones whose id did not match. But the data had already arrived over the websocket, where anyone can read it in devtools. The code comment calls it a client-side `if` hiding a data leak, not preventing one. The fix passes `filter: { id: { eq: projectId } }` so the server only sends the visitor's own project, and keeps the local check as defence in depth.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Visitors missed their own updates with a second tab": the problem was receiving too much, not too little.
- "The worker processed each project twice": the subscription is on the client; it does not drive the worker.
- "Only wasted bandwidth": the dropped updates held other people's scope text and cost analysis, so it was a privacy leak.

excerpts.quote: Without `variables`, AppSync pushes EVERY project update to EVERY // connected client, and the check below quietly discarded the ones // that did not match.
The client-side `if` was hiding a data leak, not // preventing one.
variables: { filter: { id: { eq: projectId } } },
